newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia economy on recovery road - finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Zambia economy on recovery road - finance minister.

text.p: Zambia's economy is growing fast and the country can expect an annual growth rate of five percent over the next decade, Finance Minister Ronald Penza said on Wednesday.
Zambia has vast mineral resources but the southern African state is one of the world's poorest countries, with foreign debt of $6.4 billion and a per capita GDP of $350.
Economic reforms begun by President Frederick Chiluba's government, which won power in 1991 after 17 years of one-party rule, were paying dividends, Penza told Reuters in an interview.

"The economy is much more resilient, the economy is much "If you were here five, six years ago, this economy was so different. I am so excited that it is going where it should be, in private hands," he said.
"The private sector must have faith in the government that it will never let it down, he said, adding: "What I want from them is taxes and jobs for my people."
The country is about midway through a programme to privatise state assets, including the largest company, Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd (ZCCM).
Foreign investors were favourable towards Zambia and annual growth should average five percent to the year 2005, he said. Much of this would depend on continued private investment.
"We are confident to have, until the year 2005, an average of five percent growth in the economy.
"The confidence that we create for the private sector is so critical for the future development of Zambia," Penza said.
The government had curbed month-on-month inflation to one percent, whereas real year-on-year inflation was at around 45.6 percent in September.
He also said Zambia had received little aid this year.

Foreign donors, including the United States, Japan, Britain and Scandinavian countries, suspended support to Zambia in June over changes to the constitution which excluded former president Kenneth Kaunda from elections scheduled for November 18.
But Penza said Zambia still continued to service foreign debt, now at $6.4 billion, down from $7.4 billion in 1991 when Chiluba beat Kaunda in elections.
"In 1996 we have had very little donor support, but we have been current with our debt service repayments. And this has largely been due to policy reforms," he said.
Zambia also plans to reduce dependence on copper exports, the lifeblood of the economy, which account for 80 percent of foreign exchange earnings.
"My strategy over the next five years is to expand non-metal exports so that they take over the gap both in terms of donor support and metal-driven exports," Penza said.
Zambia's 1995 exports were valued at $1.19 billion. Imports stood at $1.28 billion.
The government wants to speed up the sale of ZCCM, which could see up to 15,000 employees lose their jobs as part of the privatisation.
"My government in 1997 will be moving more strongly on privatisation of ZCCM. That is very, very important," Penza said.
The Zambia Privatisation Agency said last week 39 companies were in the running for ZCCM's copper mining and power assets.
